questions.hint: Could there be more than one use for a cursor sprite?
questions.title: [Select one] Why might a cursor sprite be used in this game?

answers.text: To help the player visualize where they are placing the towers on the tilemap when creating their defense.
To select a level on the level select screen.
To select towers from the inventory menu.

questions.correctResponse: Using a cursor sprite to provide the user with visual feedback when designing levels, using inventory items and more can really improve the user experience.

questions.hint: What makes a game strategic? How could the towers be coded to add a strategic element to the game?
questions.title: [Select one] When coding Tower Defense, you will create multiple tower options of different sizes that can fire projectiles at enemies. To create an exciting and strategic game, these towers should….

answers.text: All have projectiles that follow enemy sprites when fired so every tower has a 100% chance of finding and destroying an enemy. This would make the game’s money and inventory system irrelevant, and provide the user with the best possible gaming experience.

Have different projectile velocity and sprite detection range, and be priced accordingly. This would encourage the user to think about the benefits of fewer, more powerful towers vs many, less powerful towers.
Shake after firing a projectile. This makes the game much more visually exciting and greatly affects the users game strategy.

questions.correctResponse: Are there other customizations you could add to increase the strategic thinking needed for this game?

questions.hint: How else might enemies of varying strength be shown?
questions.title: [Select one] The only way to show enemies of varying strength or difficulty is with a status bar.
questions.correctResponse: In Tower Defense, enemies will be color-coded to show their strength!
